title: Where Idioms Come From
text:
Idioms often appear to defy logic, yet most of them preserve traces of the material culture that spawned them. Expressions such as 'to let the cat out of the bag' or 'to spill the beans' seem arbitrary until one considers the domestic settings in which they arose. Etymologists, however, caution that many popular explanations are apocryphal, and that the true provenance of an idiom is frequently obscured by centuries of retelling. Consequently, the genealogy of a phrase tends to be a matter of plausible reconstruction rather than documented certainty.

Nevertheless, the appeal of origin stories lies less in their accuracy than in the satisfaction they provide. A tidy anecdote allows speakers to feel that a figurative expression is anchored in concrete experience, which in turn lends it a certain authority. Scholars therefore distinguish between the historical record and the folk etymology that circulates alongside it. Both, in their own way, reveal how communities choose to remember their language.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do etymologists warn about?
options: Many popular explanations of idioms are apocryphal
Idioms have no connection to daily life
Idioms were invented by modern writers

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do scholars distinguish between?
options: The historical record and folk etymology

questions.text: What can be inferred about why people find origin stories appealing?
options: They make figurative language seem grounded in real experience
They replace the need for dictionaries
They are usually confirmed by documents

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the status of idiom origins in general?
options: They are often reconstructed rather than firmly documented
They are fully recorded in official archives
They are impossible to discuss meaningfully
They are the same for all languages

paragraph_translations: Las expresiones idiomáticas suelen parecer contrarias a la lógica, pero la mayoría conserva huellas de la cultura material que les dio origen. Frases como 'to let the cat out of the bag' o 'to spill the beans' parecen arbitrarias hasta que se considera el entorno doméstico en el que surgieron. Sin embargo, los etimólogos advierten que muchas explicaciones populares son apócrifas, y que la procedencia real de una expresión suele quedar oculta tras siglos de repetición. En consecuencia, la genealogía de una frase suele ser una reconstrucción plausible más que una certeza documentada.

No obstante, el atractivo de las historias sobre el origen reside menos en su exactitud que en la satisfacción que ofrecen. Una anécdota ordenada permite a los hablantes sentir que una expresión figurada está anclada en una experiencia concreta, lo que a su vez le confiere cierta autoridad. Por ello, los estudiosos distinguen entre el registro histórico y la etimología popular que circula junto a él. Ambos, a su manera, revelan cómo las comunidades deciden recordar su lengua.
